proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(j\in I\).  By Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:anm\text{-}equations}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:noise\text{-}exogeneity}\),
\[
m_{j,\theta_j}(C_j)=f_j(C_j)+\mathbb E_P\varepsilon_j,
\qquad
r_{j,\theta_j}=\varepsilon_j-\mathbb E_P\varepsilon_j\perp C_j.
\]
Thus the joint law of \((C_j,r_{j,\theta_j})\) equals the product of its marginals.  Definition \(\mathrm{def:hsic}\) then gives \(H_{j,\theta_j}=0\).

For completeness, the Gaussian-kernel implication used in the reverse direction follows directly from Fourier analysis.  If \(\nu=R_{UV}-R_U\otimes R_V\), then Fubini's theorem, applicable because the kernels are bounded, gives
\[
\left\|\mu_R-\mu_{R_U\otimes R_V}\right\|_{\mathcal H_{k\otimes\ell}}^2
=c_{\sigma_K}\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\widehat\nu(\omega_1,\omega_2)|^2
e^{-\sigma_K^2(\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2)/2}\,d\omega_1d\omega_2.
\]
The weight is strictly positive.  Hence a zero norm implies \(\widehat\nu=0\) almost everywhere and, by continuity, everywhere.  Convolving \(\nu\) with a centered Gaussian of variance \(\eta^2\) gives a signed density whose Fourier transform is zero, so Fourier inversion makes every such convolution zero.  Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) and testing against bounded continuous functions gives \(\nu=0\).  Consequently, under Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:fixed\text{-}predictor\text{-}kernel}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:fixed\text{-}residual\text{-}kernel}\), \(H_{j,b}=0\) if and only if \(C_{j,b}\perp r_{j,b}\).

Suppose now that \(f_j\) is non-affine and, contrary to the claim, \(H_{j,-\theta_j}=0\).  The preceding equivalence and Definitions \(\mathrm{def:population\text{-}regressions}\) and \(\mathrm{def:population\text{-}residuals}\) then produce a reverse additive-noise equation
\[
C_j=m_{j,-\theta_j}(E_j)+r_{j,-\theta_j},
\qquad r_{j,-\theta_j}\perp E_j.
\]
Write \(\xi=\log p_j^C\) and \(\nu=\log p_j^\varepsilon\).  Differentiating the logarithm of the positive joint density in the forward and reverse factorizations and eliminating the reverse log densities yields, wherever \(\nu''(y-f_j(x))f_j'(x)\ne0\),
\[
\xi'''=\xi''\left(-\frac{\nu'''f_j'}{\nu''}+\frac{f_j''}{f_j'}\right)
-2\nu''f_j''f_j'+\nu'f_j'''
+\frac{\nu'\nu'''f_j''f_j'}{\nu''}
-\frac{\nu'(f_j'')^2}{f_j'}.
\]
This is exactly the differential equation excluded by Peters et al.'s Condition 19, which is imposed pairwise by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:restricted\text{-}anm}\).  Thus the reverse representation is impossible.  Since \(H_{j,-\theta_j}\) is a squared Hilbert-space norm, it is nonnegative, so it must be strictly positive.  Therefore \(\theta_j\) is the unique zero-HSIC direction.

It is enough to treat orientation \(+1\) for one pair, because coordinate swapping handles orientation \(-1\), while Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:pair\text{-}product}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def:hermite\text{-}chart}\) make all pair coordinates independent.  Put
\[
Z,\xi\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}\sim N(0,1),\qquad
Y_t=aZ+t(Z^2-1)+\tau_t\xi,qquad
\tau_t=(1-a^2-2t^2)^{1/2}.
\]
Choose a compact interval \(A=[A_0,A_1]\subset(0,1/\sqrt3)\), for example \(A_0=1/4\) and \(A_1=1/2\), and then choose \(t_0>0\) so that \(\inf_{a\in A,0\le t\le t_0}\tau_t>0\).

We first verify model membership rather than assuming it from the construction.  The cause is standard Gaussian, the noise is \(N(0,\tau_t^2)\), and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)=a^2+2t^2+\tau_t^2=1.
\]
Thus both scale normalizations hold.  The Gaussian densities are strictly positive.  Uniform lower and upper Gaussian bounds follow because \(\tau_t\) ranges in a compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\).  Taking, for instance, \(\beta=3\) and then increasing \(L\), all of \(a z+t(z^2-1)\), the Gaussian cause log density, and the Gaussian-noise log density belong uniformly to \(\mathcal H_{(2)}^\beta(L)\).  For \(t>0\), direct substitution into Condition 19 verifies the restricted condition: with \(f(z)=az+t(z^2-1)\), \(e=y-f(z)\), \(\xi''=-1\), \(\xi'''=0\), \(\nu'=-e/\tau_t^2\), \(\nu''=-1/\tau_t^2\), and \(\nu'''=0\), the right side of the excluded equation contains, at every \(z\) with \(f'(z)\ne0\), the term
\[
\frac{4t^2}{\tau_t^2f'(z)}\,y.
\]
Its coefficient is nonzero, so the equation cannot hold for all \((z,y)\).  The mechanism is nonconstant.  This proves every one-pair member property, and taking products proves \(P_{a,t,\theta}\in\mathcal M_d(\beta,L,c_0,C_0)\) for common fixed \(L,c_0,C_0\).

We next calculate the local margins.  Write \(\tau=(1-a^2)^{1/2}\), let \(p_{a,t}\) denote the density of \((Z,Y_t)\), and let \(S_a\) be its score at \(t=0\).  Since \(\dot\tau_0=0\),
\[
S_a(z,y)=\left.\partial_t\log p_{a,t}(z,y)\right|_{t=0}
=\frac{(z^2-1)(y-az)}{\tau^2}.
\]
At \(t=0\), \(Z\mid Y_0=y=ay+U\), where \(U\sim N(0,\tau^2)\).  If \(m_t(y)=\mathbb E[Z\mid Y_t=y]\), differentiation under the Gaussian integral gives
\[
\dot m_0(y)=\mathbb E[(Z-ay)S_a(Z,y)\mid Y_0=y]
=a(2-3a^2)(y^2-1).
\]
The same calculation for the conditional variance \(v_t(y)=\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid Y_t=y)\) gives
\[
\dot v_0(y)
=\mathbb E[((Z-ay)^2-\tau^2)S_a(Z,y)\mid Y_0=y]
=2\tau^2(1-3a^2)y.
\]
All differentiations are uniform for \(a\in A\), because the integrands are polynomials times Gaussian densities and \(\inf_{a\in A}\tau>0\).

Let \(R_t=Z-m_t(Y_t)\) be the reverse population residual and
\[
\Delta_{a,t}=P_{Y_t,R_t}-P_{Y_t}\otimes P_{R_t}.
\]
At \(t=0\), \(Y_0\) and \(R_0\) are independent centered Gaussians, hence \(\Delta_{a,0}=0\).  The displayed conditional-variance derivative implies
\[
\left.\partial_t\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,R_t^2)\right|_{t=0}
=\mathbb E[Y_0\dot v_0(Y_0)]
=2\tau^2(1-3a^2)\ne0.
\]
Truncating the two polynomial test functions and using Gaussian domination shows that the signed-measure derivative \(\dot\Delta_{a,0}\) is nonzero.  The Fourier identity in the proof of Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:population\text{-}direction\text{-}margin}\) is valid for finite signed measures, so its Gaussian-kernel embedding is also nonzero.  Smooth dominated differentiation of the bounded Gaussian features therefore yields, uniformly on \(A\),
\[
H_{-}(a,t)=\|\mu_{\Delta_{a,t}}\|^2
=t^2\|\mu_{\dot\Delta_{a,0}}\|^2+O(t^3)
=\kappa_H(a)t^2+O(t^3).
\]
The map \(a\mapsto\kappa_H(a)\) is continuous by the same domination argument.  It is positive throughout \(A\), and compactness gives \(\inf_{a\in A}\kappa_H(a)>0\).

In the true direction, \(m_+(Z)=aZ+t(Z^2-1)\), so
\[
q_+(a,t)=a^2+2t^2.
\]
In the reverse direction \(q_-(a,t)=\operatorname{Var}\{m_t(Y_t)\}\).  At zero, \(q_-(a,0)=a^2\).  The formula for \(\dot m_0\) is even in \(y\), whereas \(ay\) is odd; the marginal score \(\mathbb E[S_a(Z,Y_0)\mid Y_0=y]\) is odd.  Hence differentiation of \(\mathbb E[m_t(Y_t)^2]\) gives zero at \(t=0\), and uniform twice differentiability gives
\[
q_-(a,t)=a^2+O(t^2).
\]
For every \(t>0\), the true HSIC is zero and the reverse HSIC is positive by Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:population\text{-}direction\text{-}margin}\).  Definition \(\mathrm{def:gene\text{-}gain}\) consequently gives the positive-branch expansion
\[
g(a,t)=q_+(a,t)-\frac12q_-(a,t)=\frac{a^2}{2}+O(t^2).
\]

Set \(w=t^2\), and extend the positive-branch map
\[
\Psi(a,w)=(g(a,\sqrt w),H_-(a,\sqrt w))
\]
to \(w=0\) by \(\Psi(a,0)=(a^2/2,0)\).  The preceding expansions and dominated differentiation show that this is one-sided continuously differentiable and
\[
D\Psi(a,0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&\partial_w g(a,0)\\
0&\kappa_H(a)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det D\Psi(a,0)=a\kappa_H(a).
\]
The determinant is uniformly bounded away from zero on \(A\).  For a quantitative one-sided inverse argument, cover a smaller compact interval in the boundary image \(\{(a^2/2,0):a\in\operatorname{int}A\}\) by finitely many neighborhoods on which the linear part is invertible and the derivative remainder has operator norm less than half the inverse bound.  For a desired image point \(y\) in the corresponding half-rectangle, the iteration \(z_{k+1}=z_k+D\Psi(z_0)^{-1}\{y-\Psi(z_k)\}\) then has contraction ratio at most \(1/2\), stays in the neighborhood, is Cauchy, and its limit is the unique solution of \(\Psi(z)=y\).  The finite cover therefore gives common constants \(0<\underline g<\overline g<1\), \(A_H>1\), and \(\lambda_0>0\) such that every
\[
(g,h)\in[\underline g,\overline g]\times[\lambda,A_H\lambda],
\qquad 0<\lambda\le\lambda_0,
\]
equals \(\Psi(a,w)\) for some \(a\in A\) and \(0<w\le t_0^2\).  This argument also proves the asserted uniform one-sided Jacobian bound.

Finally choose these preimages independently for all \(j\in I\).  Product factorization makes the \(j\)-th two margins depend only on \((a_j,t_j)\); the true-direction HSIC is exactly zero.  Definition \(\mathrm{def:orientation\text{-}permutation}\) places those zeros and wrong-direction margins in the advertised blocks.  Therefore
\[
[\underline g,\overline g]^d\times\{0\}^d\times[\lambda,A_H\lambda]^d
\subseteq\{\Pi_\theta\Gamma_d(P_{a,t,\theta},\theta):a\in A^d,\ 0<t_j\le t_0\}
\subseteq\Pi_\theta(\mathfrak F_d),
\]
as required.

Work first in the displayed orientation.  With \(\tau=(1-a^2)^{1/2}\), the density score of \(P^+_{a,t}\) at \(t=0\) is
\[
S_a^+(x,y)=\frac{(x^2-1)(y-ax)}{\tau^2},
\]
while coordinate swapping gives
\[
S_a^-(x,y)=\frac{(y^2-1)(x-ay)}{\tau^2}.
\]
Thus the score difference is
\[
D_a(x,y)=\tau^{-2}\{(x^2-1)(y-ax)-(y^2-1)(x-ay)\}.
\]
This polynomial is not identically zero for any \(a\in(0,1)\).  Under the common centered bivariate Gaussian law \(P_{a,0}\), \(0<\mathbb E_{a,0}D_a^2<\infty\).  On the compact interval used in Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:attainable\text{-}margin\text{-}rectangle}\), continuity and compactness give
\[
0<c_D\le\mathbb E_{a,0}D_a^2\le C_D<\infty.
\]

The two density families are differentiable in quadratic mean, uniformly in this interval: their likelihood ratios are smooth functions of \((a,t,x,y)\), and every derivative for small \(t\) is bounded by a polynomial times a Gaussian density with a common nonsingular covariance envelope.  Taylor expansion in quadratic mean therefore gives, with either conventional normalization of squared Hellinger distance absorbed into the constants,
\[
h^2(P^+_{a,t},P^-_{a,t})=c_{\mathrm H}(a)t^2+O(t^3),
\qquad
\operatorname{KL}(P^+_{a,t}\Vert P^-_{a,t})=\frac{t^2}{2}\mathbb E_{a,0}D_a^2+O(t^3),
\]
where \(\inf_a c_{\mathrm H}(a)>0\).  Hence, uniformly in \(a\), both divergences are bounded above and below by fixed positive multiples of \(t^2\).

Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:attainable\text{-}margin\text{-}rectangle}\) gives
\[
H_{-\theta}(a,t)=\kappa_H(a)t^2+O(t^3),
\qquad \inf_a\kappa_H(a)>0,
\]
and places \(g(a,t)\) in the fixed navigation window after shrinking the compact \(a\)-interval and \(t_0\), if necessary.  Thus for each \(0<\lambda\le\lambda_0\) one can choose \(t=t(a,\lambda)\) with fixed constants \(0<c_t<C_t<\infty\) such that
\[
c_t\lambda\le t^2\le C_t\lambda,
\qquad \lambda\le H_{-\theta}(a,t)\le A_H\lambda.
\]
Both coordinate-swapped laws then satisfy every member property of \(\mathcal M_1(\lambda)\).  Combining the uniform Taylor bounds with \(t^2\asymp\lambda\), and using the elementary inequality \(h^2(P,Q)\le\operatorname{KL}(P\Vert Q)\), proves
\[
c\lambda\le h^2(P^+_{a,t},P^-_{a,t})
\le\operatorname{KL}(P^+_{a,t}\Vert P^-_{a,t})\le C\lambda.
\]

Fix one calibrated \(a\) and \(t=t(a,\lambda)\) from Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:mirror\text{-}information}\), and denote its two one-pair laws by \(Q_+\) and \(Q_-\).  For each \(\vartheta\in\{-1,+1\}^d\), let
\[
Q_\vartheta=\bigotimes_{j=1}^d Q_{\vartheta_j}.
\]
The proposition and Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:pair\text{-}product}\) show that every \((Q_\vartheta,\vartheta)\) belongs to the identical class \(\mathcal M_d(\lambda)\).

We first record an elementary testing inequality.  For laws \(R,S\), let \(\rho(R,S)=\int\sqrt{dR\,dS}\).  Jensen's inequality gives \(\rho(R,S)\ge e^{-\operatorname{KL}(R\Vert S)/2}\), while Cauchy--Schwarz gives \(\|R-S\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{1-\rho(R,S)^2}\).  Therefore
\[
\frac{1-\|R-S\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{2}
\ge\frac14e^{-\operatorname{KL}(R\Vert S)}.
\]
For \(n\) observations of one coordinate, Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:mirror\text{-}information}\) consequently implies that the equal-prior Bayes error \(e_n\) satisfies
\[
e_n\ge\frac14e^{-K n\lambda}
\]
for a fixed \(K\).

Under the uniform prior on \(\vartheta\), the likelihood and posterior factor over coordinates.  Exact-vector Bayes success is therefore the product of the coordinatewise Bayes successes.  Hence every estimator obeys
\[
\sup_{\vartheta}Q_\vartheta^{\otimes n}(\widetilde\theta\ne\vartheta)
\ge 1-(1-e_n)^d
\ge1-\exp\{-d e_n\}.
\]
Choose \(c_1>0\) sufficiently small relative to \(K\).  If \(\log(d+1)\ge\log(1/\alpha)\), the condition in the theorem implies \(Kn\lambda\le2Kc_1\log(d+1)\); choosing \(2Kc_1<1/2\) makes the last display exceed \(1/4\ge\alpha\), with strict inequality after decreasing \(c_1\).  If \(\log(1/\alpha)>\log(d+1)\), restrict to two vectors differing in one coordinate.  For \(\alpha\le1/16\), the bound \(e_n\ge\frac14e^{-Kn\lambda}\), with \(2Kc_1<1/3\), gives \(e_n>\alpha\).  For \(1/16<\alpha\le1/4\), Pinsker's inequality, proved by applying \((u-1)\log u\ge2(u-1)^2/(u+1)\) to the likelihood ratio, gives \(e_n\ge(1-\sqrt{Kn\lambda/2})/2>1/4\) after one further universal decrease of \(c_1\).  This proves the exact-recovery assertion for all \(d\) and \(\alpha\).

Now let \(\widetilde{\mathcal C}\) have coverage at least \(1-\alpha\), and suppose for contradiction that
\[
\sup_\vartheta Q_\vartheta^{\otimes n}(|\widetilde{\mathcal C}|>1)<c_2.
\]
Whenever the set is a singleton, output its element, and otherwise output a fixed vector.  Its error is at most \(\alpha+c_2\).  In the dimension-dominant case above, choose \(c_1\) so that the product Bayes lower bound is a fixed number larger than \(1/4+c_2\); this is a contradiction for a fixed sufficiently small \(c_2>0\).

It remains to handle the confidence-dominant case.  Take two product laws \(R_+,R_-\) differing only in the first orientation, and let \(A=\{\widetilde{\mathcal C}=\{\vartheta^+\}\}\).  Coverage and the assumed ambiguity bound imply
\[
R_+^{\otimes n}(A)\ge1-\alpha-c_2,
\qquad R_-^{\otimes n}(A)\le\alpha.
\]
The log-sum inequality applied to \(A,A^c\) yields the binary data-processing bound
\[
n\operatorname{KL}(R_+\Vert R_-)
\ge \operatorname{kl}(1-\alpha-c_2,\alpha)
\ge(1-\alpha-c_2)\log(1/\alpha)-\log2.
\]
On the other hand, the mirror bound and \(\log(1/\alpha)>\log(d+1)\) give
\[
n\operatorname{KL}(R_+\Vert R_-)
\le2Kc_1\log(1/\alpha).
\]
Choose, for example, \(c_2<1/8\) and then decrease \(c_1\) so that the last two displays are incompatible uniformly over \(0<\alpha\le1/4\).  Thus some law has non-singleton probability at least \(c_2\).  All witnesses lie in \(\mathcal M_d(\lambda)\), completing both parts.

Assume the affirmative expansion stated in the antecedent.  We prove the conditional implication exactly as stated.

First construct the conditional-risk intervals used by Definition \(\mathrm{def:simultaneous\text{-}rule}\).  On a fold independent of a fitted \(\widehat m_{j,b}\), split the held-out observations deterministically into \(K=\lceil8u\rceil\) nearly equal blocks, compute the block means of
\[
Z_i^{j,b}=\{E_{j,b}(W_i)-\widehat m_{j,b}(C_{j,b}(W_i))\}^2,
\]
and take their median; average the four rotation-specific medians and subtract the result from one to obtain \(\widehat q_{j,b}\).  This is a measurable cross-fitted squared-risk map.  The model envelope implies a common fourth-moment bound for every observed coordinate.  On \(\mathcal G_n\), Jensen's inequality and the \(L^4\) regression bound give a common conditional variance bound for \(Z_i^{j,b}\).  Moreover, conditional-mean orthogonality and the unit-variance assumptions give the exact identity
\[
1-\mathbb E[Z_i^{j,b}\mid\widehat m_{j,b}]
=q_{j,b}-\|\widehat m_{j,b}-m_{j,b}\|_{L^2(P_{C_{j,b}})}^2.
\]
Chebyshev's inequality on each block makes its failure probability at most \(1/8\) after multiplying the deviation by a fixed constant; the binomial expansion for a majority of bad blocks bounds the median failure by \(2e^{-u}\).  A union bound over \(2d\) queries, with \(u=x+\log(2d)\), therefore yields simultaneous intervals
\[
|\widehat q_{j,b}-q_{j,b}|
\le R_q(u):=C_q\left\{\left(r_n+\sqrt{u/n}\right)^2+\sqrt{u/n}\right\}
\]
outside an event of probability at most \(2e^{-x}\).  This derivation uses only the stated \(L^4\) good event, and the construction is available whenever \(u\le c n\).  Since an expansion valid for \(c_u\) remains valid after decreasing \(c_u\), take \(c_u\) small enough that \(R_q(u)\le\underline g/4\) whenever \(u\le c_un\).

Set \(x=x_\alpha=\log(8/\alpha)\) and \(u=u_{d,\alpha}\).  There are numerical constants \(c_*,C_*\) such that
\[
c_*\log((d+1)/\alpha)\le u\le C_*\log((d+1)/\alpha).
\]
Because \(0<\lambda\le1\), choosing \(C\ge C_*/c_u\) makes \(n\lambda\ge C\log((d+1)/\alpha)\) imply \(u\le c_un\).

On the joint HSIC and conditional-risk event, the affirmative expansion and \(H_{j,-\theta_j}\le A_H\lambda\) give
\[
|\widehat H_{j,-\theta_j}^{\perp}-H_{j,-\theta_j}|
\le C_H\left(\sqrt{A_H\lambda u/n}+u/n+r_n^4\right),
\]
while \(H_{j,\theta_j}=0\) gives
\[
|\widehat H_{j,\theta_j}^{\perp}|
\le C_H(u/n+r_n^4).
\]
Increase \(C\) and decrease \(c_r\), using \(n\lambda\ge Cu\) and \(r_n^4\le c_r\lambda\), so both radii are at most \(\lambda/3\).  Hence the true-direction interval contains zero and the wrong-direction interval neither contains zero nor misses its true value in \([\lambda,A_H\lambda]\).  The candidate-oriented score contrast is \(q_{j,\theta_j}-q_{j,-\theta_j}/2=g_j\); its interval radius is at most \(3R_q(u)/2<\underline g\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:navigation\text{-}window}\) therefore makes its lower endpoint nonnegative.  Thus \(B_j=\{\theta_j\}\) for every \(j\).

The affirmative HSIC event fails with probability at most \(2e^{-x_\alpha}=\alpha/4\), and the conditional-risk event has the same bound.  Therefore the joint event has probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\), in particular at least \(1-\alpha\).  On it \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_n=\{\theta\}\) and \(\widehat\theta_n=\theta\), proving the uniform upper bound.

Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:product\text{-}testing\text{-}converse}\) gives the lower bound in Definition \(\mathrm{def:minimax\text{-}frontier}\).  If
\[
n_0=\left\lceil C\lambda^{-1}\log((d+1)/\alpha)\right\rceil
\]
satisfies the displayed nuisance condition, the upper argument applies at \(n_0\).  Since \(\log((d+1)/\alpha)\ge\log8\), the ceiling is absorbed into a fixed multiplicative constant, so
\[
c_\ell\lambda^{-1}\log((d+1)/\alpha)
\le N^*(d,\alpha,\lambda)
\le n_0
\le C'\lambda^{-1}\log((d+1)/\alpha).
\]
The converse and achievability use the same \(\mathcal M_d(\lambda)\), not an oracle subclass.

Assume the affirmative expansion in the theorem's antecedent and use the measurable median-of-means conditional-risk intervals constructed in the proof of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\).  With \(x=\log(8/\alpha)\) and \(u=u_{d,\alpha}\), the affirmative residual-HSIC event and the conditional-risk event jointly have probability at least
\[
1-4e^{-x}=1-\alpha/2\ge1-\alpha.
\]
On this event every true residual-HSIC value and every \(q_{j,b}\) lies in its reported interval.

For each \(j\), Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:population\text{-}direction\text{-}margin}\) and Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:residual\text{-}hsic\text{-}window}\) give
\[
H_{j,\theta_j}=0,
\qquad H_{j,-\theta_j}\in[\lambda,A_H\lambda].
\]
Thus the interval for the true direction contains zero, and the interval for the opposite direction intersects \([\lambda,\infty)\).  After decreasing \(c_u\), as permitted because the assumed expansion remains true on a smaller range, the conditional-risk radius derived in the preceding theorem is at most \(\underline g/4\) whenever \(u\le c_un\).  The lower endpoint for
\[
q_{j,\theta_j}-\frac12q_{j,-\theta_j}=g_j\ge\underline g
\]
is consequently nonnegative.  Hence \(\theta_j\in B_j\) for every \(j\), and \(\theta\in\prod_jB_j=\widehat{\mathcal C}_n\).  This proves simultaneous coverage.

Under the two additional rate conditions, the radius calculation in Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\) makes the wrong-direction HSIC interval disjoint from zero.  Therefore \(-\theta_j\notin B_j\), while \(\theta_j\in B_j\), for all \(j\).  Hence \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_n=\{\theta\}\) on the same event and the singleton probability is at least \(1-\alpha\).

There are exactly two direction-indexed HSIC queries and two direction-indexed conditional-risk queries per pair, hence \(2d\) of each.  Every fold, clipping, ridge minimizer, block median, interval endpoint, Cartesian product, and deterministic fallback is measurable, so the set is measurable.  Each HSIC query forms only a fixed number of \(n\)-by-\(n\) kernel matrices, giving kernel-matrix cost \(O(dn^2)\).  Finally, the confidence-set part of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:product\text{-}testing\text{-}converse}\) supplies the claimed constant-factor obstruction to earlier uniform singleton collapse.

When \(d=1\), Definition \(\mathrm{def:query\text{-}universe}\) gives exactly the two queries \((1,+1)\) and \((1,-1)\), and the Cartesian product in Definition \(\mathrm{def:simultaneous\text{-}rule}\) is simply
\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}_n=\prod_{j\in\{1\}}B_j=B_1.
\]
Unpacking that definition shows that \(b\) is retained exactly under the three stated interval conditions; its last clause gives the two-direction fallback when neither candidate passes.

At the population level, Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:population\text{-}direction\text{-}margin}\) gives \(H_{1,\theta_1}=0<H_{1,-\theta_1}\), and the separated-model assumptions give \(H_{1,-\theta_1}\ge\lambda\) and \(s_{1,\theta_1}-s_{1,-\theta_1}=g_1\ge\underline g\).  Thus exactly \(\theta_1\) passes all three population conditions.

Under the affirmative expansion and the nuisance condition at \(n_0\), Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:simultaneous\text{-}graph\text{-}confidence\text{-}set}\) supplies coverage and singleton collapse, while Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:uniform\text{-}minimax\text{-}frontier}\), specialized to \(d=1\), gives
\[
N^*(1,\alpha,\lambda)\asymp\lambda^{-1}\log(2/\alpha).
\]
Both constants are independent of \(\alpha\) and \(\lambda\) over the stated local range.

theorem.statement:
The answer is negative.  For the fixed class \(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{LP}}\), there is a law \(P^\circ\in\mathcal M_1(\beta,L,c_0,C_0)\) and a constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that, for every \(C_m<\infty\), the unique admissible fit \(\widehat m\), and \(x=1\),
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}P^{\circ\otimes n}\{\mathcal G_n(1;C_m,\widehat m)^c\}\ge e^{-\delta}>2e^{-1}.
\]
Consequently no measurable statistics constructed from \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{LP}})\), and no data-dependent radii, can satisfy the probability bound posed in Open-ended Question \(\mathrm{oeq:uniform\text{-}generated\text{-}residual\text{-}expansion}\), because that bound already requires the displayed regression event.
theorem.proof_tex:
Choose one fixed nonlinear chart member \(P^\circ=P_{a,t,+}\) supplied by Theorem \(\mathrm{thm:attainable\text{-}margin\text{-}rectangle}\), with \(a\) in the interior of its compact interval and \(t>0\).  For the true-direction query, \(C=Z\sim N(0,1)\) and
\[
m(z)=az+t(z^2-1).
\]
Consider one regression fold of size \(m_n\), where \(m_n/n\to1/4\), and write \(h=h_n\).  Fix \(0<\delta<1-\log2\), so \(e^{-\delta}>2/e\).  By continuity of Gaussian tail probabilities, for every sufficiently large \(n\) there is \(z_n>0\) such that
\[
m_nP^\circ\{Z\in J_n\}=\delta,
\qquad J_n=[z_n-2h,z_n+2h].
\]
Gaussian density comparison on an interval of length \(4h\) gives
\[
z_n^2=\frac{4\beta}{2\beta+1}\log n+O(\log\log n),
\qquad z_n<T_n-h,
\]
and, for \(A_n=[z_n-h/2,z_n+h/2]\),
\[
P^\circ(Z\in A_n)\ge c/n.
\]
Here \(z_nh\to0\), so the Gaussian density varies by a factor tending to one across \(J_n\); this proves both comparisons.

Let \(E_n\) be the event that the chosen regression fold contains no predictor in \(J_n\).  Independence gives
\[
P^{\circ\otimes n}(E_n)=\left(1-\frac{\delta}{m_n}\right)^{m_n}\longrightarrow e^{-\delta}.
\]
For every \(z\in A_n\), the support of \(K_{\mathrm{LP}}((Z_i-z)/h)\) is contained in \(J_n\).  On \(E_n\) every weighted least-squares term is therefore zero.  The ridge term in Definition \(\mathrm{def:admissible\text{-}local\text{-}polynomial\text{-}class}\) makes the unique coefficient vector equal to zero, and hence \(\widehat m(z)=0\) throughout \(A_n\).  Since \(t>0\) is fixed, \(\inf_{z\in A_n}|m(z)|\ge c z_n^2\ge c'\log n\).  Consequently, on \(E_n\),
\[
\|\widehat m-m\|_{L^4(P_C)}
\ge\left(\int_{A_n}|m(z)|^4\,dP_C(z)\right)^{1/4}
\ge c''n^{-1/4}\log n.
\]
Because \(\beta>1/2\),
\[
n^{-\beta/(2\beta+1)}+n^{-1/2}=o(n^{-1/4}\log n).
\]
Thus for every fixed \(C_m\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy
\[
E_n\subseteq\mathcal G_n(1;C_m,\widehat m)^c,
\]
where \(u=1+\log2\) is fixed.  Taking lower limits proves the displayed bound.  Since the event \(\mathcal G_n^c\) is explicitly part of the union in the OEQ probability assertion, no subsequent residual-feature orthogonalization can repair this failure.
